content: 1. Risk Factors and Community Strategies for Tuberculosis (TB): Malnutrition, pneumonia, chronic lung disease, diabetes, and HIV are significant risk factors for TB. Community health strategies should integrate awareness, education, screening, prevention, and case-finding for TB in children and adolescents into training and service delivery activities. 2. WHO Policy Framework for TB Diagnostics: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a policy framework for implementing TB diagnostics, which includes recommendations for integrating advanced diagnostic tools into healthcare systems. 3. Definition of Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (XDR-TB): XDR-TB is defined as multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) that is resistant to fluoroquinolones and at least one of the Group A medicines, such as bedaquiline or linezolid. Group A medicines currently include levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid, but this classification may evolve in the future. 4. Classification of Intrathoracic Lymph Node TB in Children: Following a WHO expert consultation in 2021, intrathoracic lymph node TB is now classified as pulmonary TB in children. 5. High TB Transmission Settings: These are environments where undiagnosed or untreated TB cases are prevalent, increasing the risk of transmission. TB is most infectious when untreated or inadequately treated, and transmission is exacerbated by aerosol-generating procedures and the presence of highly susceptible individuals. 6. Household Contact and Index Case Definitions: A household contact is someone who shared the same living space with a TB patient for extended periods before the start of treatment. The index case refers to the first identified person with TB in a specific setting, although this individual may not necessarily be the source of infection. 7. Inpatient Healthcare Settings: These are facilities where patients are admitted for at least one overnight stay to receive diagnosis, treatment, and care. 8. Integrated Treatment Decision Algorithms: These are evidence-based flowcharts that help clinicians make decisions about initiating TB treatment in children based on microbiological, clinical, and radiological findings. 9. Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA): 10. Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB): MDR-TB is caused by strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistant to at least rifampicin and isoniazid. 11. New TB Cases: A new TB case refers to a person who has never been treated for TB or has taken TB medications for less than one month. 12. Non-Severe Pulmonary TB: This includes intrathoracic lymph node TB without airway obstruction, uncomplicated TB pleural effusion, or paucibacillary, non-cavitary disease confined to one lung lobe without a miliary pattern. 13. Number Needed to Screen (NNS): This refers to the number of individuals who need to be screened to diagnose one person with TB disease. 14. Operational Research in TB: This involves applied research to develop evidence for the effective and sustainable implementation of TB interventions within health systems to improve patient outcomes. 15. Systematic Screening for TB Disease: This involves identifying individuals at risk for TB in targeted populations through symptom assessment and diagnostic tests. Those who screen positive require further diagnostic confirmation. 16. Tuberculin Skin Test (TST): 17. Tuberculosis (TB) and TB Infection: TB disease refers to the clinical manifestation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, while TB infection indicates a persistent immune response to the bacteria without clinical symptoms. 18. TB Preventive Treatment (TPT): This treatment is offered to individuals at risk of developing TB disease to reduce their risk. It is also referred to as treatment of TB infection or TB preventive therapy. 19. Children and Adolescents with TB: Adolescents aged 15–19 years also represent a significant proportion of new TB cases annually. 20. Global TB Targets: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the WHO End TB Strategy aim to reduce TB incidence by 80% and TB deaths by 90% by 2030, compared to 2015 levels. 21. WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB in Children and Adolescents (2022): These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the prevention, diagnosis, and management of TB in children and adolescents. They replace the 2014 guidance and include new recommendations on diagnostic approaches, treatment regimens, and models of care. 22. Diagnostic Approaches: The Xpert Ultra test is recommended as the initial diagnostic tool for children with suspected pulmonary TB, using samples such as sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate, gastric aspirate, or stool. 23. Treatment Regimens: A 4-month treatment regimen is recommended for children with non-severe TB, while all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline or delamanid may be used for children with MDR/RR-TB. 24. Models of TB Care: Decentralized TB services and family-centered, integrated care models are recommended for children and adolescents with TB or those exposed to TB. 25. Impact of COVID-19 on TB Notifications: The COVID-19 pandemic led to a 24% decrease in TB notifications among children in 2020 compared to 2019, highlighting the need for improved case detection and management. 26. Implementation of Guidelines: The WHO operational handbook provides practical guidance on implementing the recommendations in the consolidated guidelines, including tools for integrated treatment decision-making and updated dosing for second-line TB medicines. 27. Continuous Evidence Review: WHO employs a systematic process to identify and address evidence gaps, ensuring that guidelines remain up-to-date with emerging research. These points reflect the detailed and evidence-based recommendations and strategies outlined in the WHO guidelines for managing TB in children and adolescents.
